blocks.raw: <Tip>Always verify embodied carbon values from published EPDs or lifecycle assessment databases (ICE, OneClick LCA) rather than assuming values. The actual CO2e per kilogram varies by manufacturing location, process efficiency, and transport distance. When a question provides a baseline embodied carbon for concrete (0.11 kg CO2e/kg), multiply by the percentage cement content and the percentage fly ash replacement to calculate net reduction.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Confusing EAF vs BOF Steel Emissions" severity="critical">When asked to specify recycled steel for low embodied carbon, candidates incorrectly state that all recycled steel has equal emissions. In reality, EAF (electric arc furnace) steel achieves 0.9-1.1 kg CO2e/kg via electrical melting of scrap, while BOF (blast oxygen furnace) primary steel requires 1.8-2.0 kg CO2e/kg using iron ore and coke. Recycled steel via EAF is roughly 50 percent lower carbon and is the preferred specification for low-embodied-carbon projects.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Exceeding Pozzolanic Replacement Limits" severity="high">Class F fly ash is limited to 15-25 percent dosage by weight in structural concrete per ASTM C618 guidelines; Class C is 20-35 percent. Candidates sometimes specify 40-50 percent fly ash replacement, which may result in slower early strength gain and reduced durability due to incomplete pozzolanic reaction. Always confirm replacement percentage aligns with concrete strength class and early-age strength requirements.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Assuming Recycled Aggregates Meet Structural Standards" severity="high">Recycled concrete aggregates (RCA) can substitute for virgin aggregates in non-structural fill and base courses when meeting ASTM C33 gradation. However, RCA exhibits higher absorption (3-8%) versus virgin aggregate (0.5-1%), affecting long-term durability and strength. Recycled aggregates are not suitable for primary structural concrete without additional testing and strength verification; candidates must recognize this limitation to avoid over-specifying reuse.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw:
• Forgetting to multiply cement content (%) by cement embodied carbon (kg CO2e/kg) before calculating reduction
  • Confusing kilograms of material with percentage composition in a concrete mix design
  • Assuming zero embodied carbon for fly ash or slag (they have small positive values, ~0.05-0.15 kg CO2e/kg)
  • Applying the same embodied carbon value to both Class F and Class C fly ash (Class C typically has 10-15% higher emissions due to calcium oxide content)
  • Using embodied carbon values from international databases without accounting for local transport distance and fuel type in the Philippines
